title: Business Intelligence Platforms: A Practical Evaluation Guide
description: How to compare BI platforms through metric governance, data quality, access control, self-service analysis, and total cost.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Start with decisions and users
sections.body: List the recurring decisions the BI platform must improve, the people making them, and the time frame in which the data must be available. Interview analysts, operational managers, and executives because each group may need different levels of detail. Identify the existing reports that are trusted, those maintained manually, and those that disagree. Define a small set of priority questions and the business action each answer should inform. Buying a visualization tool before resolving these needs often creates more dashboards without improving decisions.

sections.title: Establish metric definitions and data quality
sections.body: Create a shared definition for key measures, including numerator, denominator, filters, time zone, refresh frequency, and owner. Check completeness, duplication, freshness, and reconciliation with the source system. Determine where transformations live and how a change to a definition is reviewed. During a pilot, compare the platform's results with a known source report and investigate every material discrepancy. A polished chart is not useful if different departments interpret the same metric differently.

sections.title: Evaluate data modeling and integration
sections.body: Map the required databases, warehouses, spreadsheets, SaaS systems, and refresh schedules. Test connector reliability, incremental refresh, schema changes, joins, and handling of late-arriving data. Confirm whether business logic can be versioned and reviewed, and whether analysts can reuse governed datasets instead of recreating calculations in every report. Evaluate query performance with representative data volumes. If the platform requires a large manual preparation step every week, include that maintenance burden in the comparison.

sections.title: Design access and governance
sections.body: Decide who can view, edit, share, export, and administer each dataset and report. Test row-level and column-level restrictions using accounts that represent real roles. Check audit logs, sharing defaults, external access, data residency, retention, and deletion. Define a certification process for trusted dashboards and a way to retire stale reports. Self-service should make analysis easier without letting sensitive data spread through uncontrolled copies.

sections.title: Test self-service and adoption
sections.body: Ask a business user to answer a real question without help from the analyst who built the dashboard. Observe whether they can find the right metric, apply filters, understand caveats, and export or share results safely. Measure task success, time to answer, support requests, and the number of conflicting reports created. Provide definitions and explanations near the data. Adoption is not simply the number of accounts provisioned; it is whether users can make correct decisions from the information.

sections.title: Compare cost and performance
sections.body: Include licenses by role, viewer limits, data storage, query or refresh usage, embedded analytics, premium connectors, administration, and training. Test typical and peak workloads, including the cost of concurrent queries. Check export formats and whether models or dashboards can be migrated if the contract ends. Compare the cost of the platform with the ongoing analyst effort required to prepare and reconcile data. Use a forecast based on your own usage, not a generic vendor example.

sections.title: Pilot, roll out, and govern
sections.body: Select one high-value reporting area with a named business owner and data owner. Agree on acceptance criteria for correctness, freshness, access control, response time, and user task success. Document source lineage, definitions, permissions, and support ownership before expanding. Review dashboard usage and trust after launch, remove duplicate reports, and update definitions through a controlled process. Reassess the platform when data volume, governance requirements, or user needs change.
